individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper presents DexMan, an automated pipeline that converts monocular RGB videos of human bimanual manipulation into dexterous skills for a full humanoid robot in simulation. It reconstructs 3D objects, estimates hand/object poses from video, retargets motions to a humanoid with two dexterous hands, and trains a residual RL policy with a contact-prior attraction reward. Experiments show improved object pose estimation on TACO, higher success rate than MANIPTRANS on OakInk-v2, and end-to-end skill acquisition from real and synthetic videos.
Strengths: First framework to directly control a full humanoid robot with two dexterous hands from uncalibrated monocular RGB videos, without requiring mocap data, 3D assets, or motion annotations.

The contact-prior attraction reward is an interesting and well-motivated solution to noisy reference motions; its object-centric formulation addresses limitations of prior contact rewards that use nearest-surface or fixed-coordinate cues.
The pipeline is modular and includes practical engineering solutions such as stable object configuration sampling and object-centric depth alignment for temporal consistency.
Demonstrates the ability to generate training data from synthetic videos (Veo3), which is important for scaling robot skill acquisition beyond mocap datasets.
Ablation studies confirm the critical importance of the contact reward and the stable configuration sampling for downstream RL success.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited: pose estimation is compared against only FoundationPose and SpatialTracker; RL is compared against only MANIPTRANS, which uses a different embodiment (floating hands) and may not constitute a controlled comparison.
The full video-to-robot pipeline is not compared with any baseline; success rates are low (27.4% on TACO and 39% on synthetic videos), and the paper does not report variance or confidence intervals.
Several components require manual intervention (target object identification, table detection, scale alignment), so the claim of full automation is overstated.

The imitation reward formula appears to contain a typo (the rotational term reuses Delta_pos), and the contact reward relies on several manually tuned thresholds and weights without sensitivity analysis.
The system is only tested in simulation; there is a substantial sim-to-real gap, and the failure case analysis reveals limitations in grasp quality and in-hand manipulation.

The 'w/o contact reward' ablation shows improved E_r/E_t and IoU despite much lower success rate, indicating that these secondary metrics may be biased by easier successful trajectories and are not reliable proxies.
Questions: How are target objects identified in the videos? The paper says manually identified; does this manual step limit the claimed automation and scalability?
What is the variance/seed-sensitivity of the RL success rates? None of the tables include confidence intervals or multiple seeds.
In the TACO pose-estimation experiments, are ground-truth 3D object models used or are reconstructed meshes used? If reconstructed, how does mesh quality affect the reported metrics?
Why does removing the contact reward produce lower E_r and E_t and higher IoU while success rate collapses? Does this indicate that these metrics are only computed on a few easy successful rollouts?
How sensitive is the contact reward to the threshold tau_j and the weighting factors? Were these tuned per task or fixed across all tasks?
The imitation reward formula in Section 3.4 appears to use Delta_pos in the rotational term; is this a typo and should it be Delta_rot?
Can the pipeline handle multiple objects, occlusions, or significant hand-object occlusions, which are common in natural videos?
Why is there no comparison with other RGB-video-based methods such as OKAMI or DexMV in the full pipeline evaluation?
Limitations: The framework is developed and evaluated only in simulation, leaving a large sim-to-real gap for physical humanoid deployment.
The assumptions are restrictive: single human demonstrator, rigid tabletop objects, and stationary camera; deformable or articulated objects are not supported.
Target objects are manually identified, which limits full automation and scalability to unconstrained videos.
The end-effector control parameterization ignores full arm posture, which is important for collision avoidance and coordinated multi-arm manipulation.
Hand and object poses are estimated in a decoupled manner before contact-prior extraction, which may propagate inconsistencies and compromise contact reasoning.
The success rates on raw video inputs are low (27.4% and 39%), and there are no baselines for the full video-to-robot pipeline, making it difficult to benchmark the improvement.
The paper does not analyze negative societal impacts, though the use of large-scale human videos for robot skill learning may raise privacy or dual-use concerns.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: DexMan is an automated framework that converts monocular RGB human videos of rigid-object manipulation into bimanual dexterous manipulation policies for a simulated humanoid robot. The pipeline reconstructs 3D objects, estimates depth and hand/object poses, retargets human motion to the robot, and trains a residual RL policy guided by imitation, object-following, and a newly proposed contact-prior attraction reward. The paper reports state-of-the-art object pose estimation on TACO, a 19% absolute success-rate improvement over MANIPTRANS on OakInk-v2, and the first full video-to-robot skill acquisition results on both TACO and Veo3-generated synthetic videos.
Strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: learning bimanual dexterous skills for a full humanoid robot from monocular RGB video, without requiring camera calibration, depth sensors, scanned 3D assets, or ground-truth hand/object annotations.

The contact-prior attraction reward is a thoughtful contribution; it uses keypoint-vertex correspondences and directional alignment rather than naive proximity or world-coordinate rewards, and ablations show it is critical for learning.
Demonstrates results on both real (TACO) and synthetic (Veo3) videos, suggesting a scalable path for generating training data.
The method controls a full humanoid robot with two dexterous hands rather than simplified floating hands, and the failure-case analysis honestly discusses embodiment-gap limitations.
Ablations of reward components and stable object-pose sampling provide useful insight into the design choices.
Weaknesses: The OakInk-v2 comparison with MANIPTRANS is not apples-to-apples: the paper changes the evaluation protocol from MANIPTRANS's intermediate-frame success to whole-episode success, yet does not report MANIPTRANS under the same protocol. The claimed 19% improvement may be partly an artifact of this metric change.

Pose estimation is evaluated against only two baselines (FoundationPose and SpatialTracker) on TACO, which is not a standard 6D pose benchmark. The 'state-of-the-art' claim is not well supported by a broader comparison.

In the full video-to-robot experiments, no baseline is compared, and success is measured against the estimated object trajectory (via IoU with rendered masks). Since the policy is trained to follow that same estimated trajectory, the success rate may reflect overfitting to noisy pose estimates rather than genuine task completion.

Several technical details are missing or unclear: the imitation reward equation appears to have a typo (the second term uses Delta_pos instead of Delta_rot); the IK conversion of wrist residuals to full joint commands is not fully specified; and the effect of stable-configuration sampling on final RL performance is not reported, only the percentage of stable placements.
The absolute success rates on TACO (27.4%) and synthetic videos (39.0%) are low; without a baseline, it is difficult to judge whether this is a meaningful advance or merely a proof-of-concept.

The claim of eliminating ground-truth motion annotations is only validated on a small subset (50 TACO and 50 synthetic sequences), and the OakInk-v2 experiments still use ground-truth poses and assets.
Questions: How is task success defined in the full video-to-robot experiments when ground-truth object motion is unavailable? Is success determined by matching the estimated object trajectory, and if so, what prevents the policy from overfitting to pose-estimation errors?
On OakInk-v2, why was the evaluation protocol changed from MANIPTRANS's intermediate-frame success to whole-episode success? What success rate does MANIPTRANS achieve under the new protocol?
Can you compare pose estimation against more recent generalizable 6D pose estimators, and report per-sequence or per-object breakdowns on TACO?

How are the keypoint-vertex contact pairs extracted in practice, and what fraction of frames yield no valid contact candidates due to noisy hand/object poses? How sensitive are the results to the distance thresholds tau_j?
The imitation reward equation in Section 3.4 seems to use Delta_pos twice; should the second term be Delta_rot? Please clarify.
How are the wrist residual targets converted to joint angles via IK, and does the IK solver account for self-collision or arm posture beyond wrist position/orientation?
What is the effect of stable object configuration sampling on final RL success rates, not just on the percentage of stable initial configurations?
Have you tested the policy on a real robot, and what specific sim-to-real gap remains?
Limitations: The method is developed and evaluated entirely in simulation; no physical robot deployment is attempted, leaving a substantial sim-to-real gap.
The framework assumes a single human demonstrator and rigid tabletop objects; it cannot handle deformable, articulated, or multi-agent interactions.
Hand and object poses are estimated separately in a sequential pipeline, which can produce inconsistent contact priors and propagate errors.
The end-effector/IK control parameterization does not explicitly optimize full arm posture, which is important for collision avoidance and multi-arm coordination.
Success rates on real and synthetic videos remain low (27.4% and 39.0%), and the reference object trajectory itself is noisy, limiting real-world applicability.

Potential negative societal impacts are not discussed; while not immediate, advancing video-to-robot skill transfer could lower barriers to autonomous dexterous manipulation, with dual-use implications.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: DexMan is an automated framework that converts monocular RGB videos of human bimanual manipulation into dexterous manipulation skills for a full humanoid robot (Unitree G1 with Shadow hands) in simulation. The pipeline reconstructs 3D objects from video, estimates hand and object poses using existing components (SAM2, Trellis, VGGT, HaMeR, FoundationPose, SpatialTracker), retargets human motions to the robot, and trains a residual RL policy with a novel contact-prior attraction reward. The paper evaluates object pose estimation on TACO, residual RL on OakInk-v2, and full video-to-robot skill acquisition on real TACO videos and synthetic Veo3-generated videos, reporting improved success rates over baselines and ablations showing the importance of the contact reward.
Strengths: Addresses an important problem: scaling dexterous bimanual manipulation skills from readily available monocular RGB videos without mocap or ground-truth annotations.

Proposes a complete pipeline integrating state-of-the-art modules (Trellis, VGGT, HaMeR, FoundationPose, SpatialTracker, Isaac Gym) and demonstrates the first full-humanoid bimanual dexterous manipulation from monocular RGB input.
The contact-prior attraction reward is well-motivated, object-centric, and shows substantial gains in the ablations (success rate drops from 27.4% to 7.2% on TACO without it).
The framework is shown to work on both real videos (TACO) and synthetic videos (Veo3), suggesting a path to large-scale data generation.
The stable object configuration sampling is a simple but effective contribution that improves simulation setup reliability.
Weaknesses: The pose estimation comparison is not fully convincing: only two baselines are used, no error bars or statistical significance are reported, and DexMan's temporal stability (0.76) is actually worse than SpatialTracker (0.79), contradicting the claim of consistent superiority.

The RL comparison with MANIPTRANS is not a controlled experiment: DexMan controls a full humanoid with two Shadow hands, while MANIPTRANS uses floating hands. The evaluation protocol is also altered (entire episode vs intermediate frames), making the 19% improvement difficult to attribute solely to the contact reward.

The claim of being the 'first framework' to derive bimanual dexterous skills from monocular RGB is overclaimed, as prior works like DexMV and DexVip already learn from RGB videos, even if with simplified embodiments.

The video-to-robot success rates are low (27.4% on TACO, 39.0% on synthetic), and there is no comparison to simpler baselines such as executing the retargeted motion without RL or using alternative contact reward formulations in the same pipeline.

The contact reward fails on concave objects (as admitted in the shoe-picking failure case): it only attracts keypoints to vertices without considering the correct side of the surface, leading to spurious local optima.

The pipeline is not fully automated: target objects must be manually identified, and details about video sequence selection (e.g., why 50 of 244 TACO sequences) are missing, limiting reproducibility and scalability.
Questions: In the pose estimation experiments, does FoundationPose receive the same input depth as DexMan (estimated by VGGT) or the ground-truth depth from TACO? How are object masks provided to each baseline?
What is the statistical significance of the pose estimation improvements? Were standard deviations or multiple runs reported? Why is the temporal stability of DexMan lower than SpatialTracker's?

Was MANIPTRANS retrained using the exact same compute, reward weights, and network architecture as in its original paper? Could the observed success-rate gap be due to the different embodiment or evaluation protocol rather than the contact reward?
How were the 50 TACO sequences and 50 Veo3 synthetic videos selected? Were they random? Could selection bias inflate the reported success rates?
What is the success rate of the pure retargeted policy without RL? This baseline would quantify the contribution of RL and the contact reward.

In the video-to-robot experiments, is the trajectory-to-mask IoU computed over the entire episode or only successful rollouts, and how is the rendered object mask obtained? Could this metric be trivially high for static objects?
Limitations: The system is evaluated only in simulation, leaving a substantial sim-to-real gap.
The method assumes single human demonstrations with rigid, textureless tabletop objects; it does not handle deformable or articulated objects.
Target objects must be manually identified in the input video, which limits full automation and scalability.
The contact reward is prone to local optima for objects with concave or hollow geometries (e.g., shoes, cups), as acknowledged in the failure cases.
The sequential pipeline (reconstruction → pose estimation → retargeting → RL) may accumulate errors from each stage, affecting downstream policy learning.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper presents DexMan, an automated framework for converting monocular RGB videos of human bimanual manipulation into dexterous robot skills for a humanoid robot in simulation. The pipeline reconstructs 3D objects, estimates hand and object poses, retargets motions to a humanoid with dual dexterous hands, and trains a residual RL policy with a novel contact-aware reward. The framework is evaluated on object pose estimation (TACO), RL policy learning (OakInk-v2), and full video-to-robot transfer from real and synthetic videos, showing state-of-the-art pose estimation and improved policy success rates, with ablations demonstrating the importance of the contact reward.
Strengths: Novel full pipeline from monocular RGB video to full humanoid bimanual dexterous manipulation, eliminating the need for mocap, depth, or 3D assets.

Contact-based reward that uses object-centric correspondences significantly improves policy learning from noisy video-derived motion priors (success rate gains of ~19% on OakInk-v2 and ~20% in ablations).
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks and both real and synthetic videos, with ablations and failure-case analysis.
Demonstrates scalability by using synthetic videos (Veo3) as data source, which could enable large-scale data generation.
Technical contributions in object pose estimation (using 3D point trajectories to stabilize FoundationPose) and stable placement of reconstructed objects in simulation.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is only in simulation; no real-robot or sim-to-real experiments are provided, limiting practical applicability.
Success rates remain low (27.4% on TACO, 44.3% on OakInk-v2), suggesting limited reliability of the learned skills.
Comparison on OakInk-v2 with MANIPTRANS (floating hands) may not isolate the benefit from the full humanoid embodiment; no ablation with floating hands is provided.

The pipeline is a sequential integration of many off-the-shelf components; errors in depth, hand pose, object pose, and reconstruction can propagate, and the paper does not quantify per-stage error contributions.

Contact reward can still converge to local optima (e.g., thumb contacting the outside of a concave object) as noted in failure cases, and does not explicitly enforce approaching from the correct side.
There are typos in equations (e.g., imitation reward uses 'pos' in the rotation term) and some details are only in appendices, making reproduction harder.
Questions: How does the policy performance degrade if ground-truth hand poses are used instead of HaMeR estimates? This would help isolate the impact of hand pose noise.
In the OakInk-v2 comparison, does DexMan also improve over a version with floating hands? What is the drop in success rate when controlling the full humanoid compared to floating hands?
What are the main failure modes in the TACO video-to-robot experiments? Are they due to pose estimation errors, retargeting mistakes, or embodiment limitations?
How sensitive are the results to the reward weights and thresholds? Is there a range where performance is stable?
How were the 50 TACO sequences and 50 Veo3 prompts selected? Is there a potential selection bias?
What is the computational cost of the entire pipeline (pose estimation, RL training) and the wall-clock time per task?
Could the stable configuration sampling be improved by using physics-optimization instead of random perturbation?

review.Summary: The paper presents DexMan, an automated framework for converting monocular RGB human demonstration videos into bimanual dexterous manipulation policies for a full humanoid robot in simulation. It reconstructs 3D objects, estimates depth, hand and object poses, retargets motions, and trains residual RL with contact-based rewards. Experiments report improved object pose accuracy on TACO and higher success than MANIPTRANS on OakInk-v2, plus full video-to-skill results on TACO and Veo3 synthetic videos.
Strengths: Addresses a significant and timely problem: learning bimanual dexterous manipulation from monocular RGB video without ground-truth labels or mocap.
The proposed contact-prior attraction reward is a sensible object-centric alternative to prior contact rewards and appears to be the key contributor in ablations.
The pose estimation stage leverages 3D point trajectories to stabilize FoundationPose, yielding large reductions in failure rate on TACO.
The full pipeline is demonstrated on both real and synthetic videos, suggesting a scalable data-generation direction.
Paper is generally well structured with detailed appendix on implementation.
Weaknesses: The RL comparison is not apples-to-apples: MANIPTRANS uses floating hands while DexMan uses a full humanoid, and MANIPTRANS is not retargeted or retrained on the same embodiment; the 19% gain may partly reflect different training details rather than the contact reward.

The pose-estimation evaluation is limited to only two baselines (FoundationPose and SpatialTracker), and the paper claims state-of-the-art without comparing to other recent 6D pose estimators or reporting statistical significance.

Full video-to-robot experiments rely on a hand-selected subset of 50 TACO and 50 synthetic videos; no details on selection criteria or task difficulty, and no baseline comparison, so success rates (27.4% and 39.0%) are difficult to interpret.

The contact reward is sensitive to thresholds and weights, but there are no ablations on tau_j or lambda_c; the paper also notes a failure case caused by a reward local optimum where the hand touches the wrong side of an object.
The imitation reward formula appears to have a typo (uses Delta_pos for rotation instead of Delta_rot), which harms reproducibility.
No real-robot experiments; the paper acknowledges the sim-to-real gap but the claimed skills remain in simulation.
Low success rates on in-the-wild videos (27.4% on TACO) suggest the method is far from practical scalability.
Questions: How is the RL success threshold applied for full episodes? If all timesteps must stay below the thresholds, can small initial pose misalignment make success impossible, and what were the exact MANIPTRANS evaluation settings used for comparison?

Could the gains on OakInk-v2 be due partly to controlling a full humanoid with the lower body fixed versus floating hands? Did you compare your method on floating hands or retarget MANIPTRANS to the same humanoid embodiment?
What were the selection criteria for the 50 TACO sequences and 50 Veo3 synthetic videos? Are these the easiest tasks, and how would the success rates change on a random or more diverse subset?

How sensitive is the contact reward to the distance thresholds tau_j and the weights lambda_c? Was there any ablation of these hyperparameters, and what happens when no contact candidates exist early in training?
The paper uses VGGT and HaMeR for depth and hand poses; do these methods require known camera intrinsics or can they handle arbitrary monocular videos without calibration?
The pose estimation table shows DexMan has lower temporal stability than SpatialTracker (0.76 vs 0.79). Why is this not a concern, and does temporal stability affect downstream RL performance?
For the full video-to-robot pipeline, what are the per-task success rates? Are successes concentrated in simple pick-and-place tasks rather than complex articulated manipulations?
Limitations: Simulation-only; no physical robot deployment, leaving a substantial sim-to-real gap.
Assumes a single human, rigid objects, and tabletop scenes; no deformable or articulated objects.
Target objects are manually identified, so the pipeline is not fully automated.
Hand and object poses are estimated separately, which can produce inconsistent contact priors.
Only a small hand-selected subset is used for the full video evaluation, so success rates may not generalize.
The contact reward can converge to local optima, e.g., contacting the wrong surface, as shown in the shoe-picking failure case.
The end-effector control ignores the full arm posture, limiting collision avoidance and multi-arm coordination.

review.Summary: DexMan is an automated framework that converts monocular RGB videos of human bimanual manipulation into dexterous manipulation skills for a full humanoid robot (Unitree G1 with Shadow hands) in simulation. The pipeline reconstructs 3D objects, estimates depth and hand/object poses, retargets human motion, and trains a residual RL policy guided by imitation, object-following, and a newly proposed contact-prior attraction reward. The paper reports improved object pose estimation on TACO, a higher success rate than MANIPTRANS on OakInk-v2, and full video-to-robot skill acquisition results on both real TACO videos and synthetic Veo3-generated videos, with ablations showing the importance of the contact reward.
Strengths: Addresses a significant and timely problem: learning bimanual dexterous manipulation for a full humanoid robot from monocular RGB video without needing mocap, 3D assets, or ground-truth annotations.

The contact-prior attraction reward is a thoughtful, object-centric contribution that clearly improves policy learning from noisy reference motions; ablations show a substantial drop in success rate without it.

The modular pipeline integrates state-of-the-art components (Trellis, VGGT, HaMeR, FoundationPose, SpatialTracker, Isaac Gym) and demonstrates the first full-humanoid bimanual dexterous manipulation from monocular RGB input.
The ability to leverage synthetic videos (Veo3) as a data source suggests a scalable path for generating large-scale training data.
The stable object configuration sampling is a practical engineering contribution that improves simulation setup reliability.
The failure-case analysis honestly discusses embodiment-gap limitations and helps identify future research directions.
Weaknesses: The pose-estimation evaluation is limited to only two baselines (FoundationPose and SpatialTracker) on TACO, which is not a standard 6D pose benchmark, and no statistical significance or error bars are reported; the temporal stability is actually worse than SpatialTracker, contradicting claims of consistent superiority.

The RL comparison with MANIPTRANS is not apples-to-apples: DexMan controls a full humanoid with two Shadow hands while MANIPTRANS uses floating hands, and the evaluation protocol is changed (intermediate-frame success vs whole-episode success), making the claimed 19% improvement difficult to attribute solely to the approach.

The full video-to-robot pipeline is not compared against any baseline, and success rates on real videos (27.4%) and synthetic videos (39.0%) are low; without a baseline, it is unclear whether this is a meaningful advance or a proof-of-concept.
The claim of full automation is overstated: target objects are manually identified, and details about video sequence selection (e.g., why 50 of 244 TACO sequences) and scale alignment are missing.

Reproducibility is harmed by a typo in the imitation reward equation (the rotational term uses Delta_pos instead of Delta_rot), and several hyperparameters (distance thresholds tau_j, reward weights lambda_c) lack sensitivity analysis.
The system is only evaluated in simulation; there is no real-robot deployment or sim-to-real analysis, leaving a substantial gap in practical applicability.

The contact reward is prone to local optima for concave or hollow objects (e.g., shoes, cups), as acknowledged in the failure cases, and it does not enforce approaching from the correct side of the surface.

The successful trajectories used to compute secondary metrics (E_r, E_t, IoU) may be biased because the 'w/o contact reward' ablation shows better values on these metrics despite a much lower success rate, indicating they are not reliable proxies for task success.
Questions: How is task success defined in the full video-to-robot experiments when ground-truth object motion is unavailable? Is success determined by matching the estimated object trajectory, and if so, what prevents the policy from overfitting to pose-estimation errors?

In the OakInk-v2 comparison, why was the evaluation protocol changed from MANIPTRANS's intermediate-frame success to whole-episode success? What success rate does MANIPTRANS achieve under the new protocol?
How were the 50 TACO sequences and 50 Veo3 synthetic videos selected? Are they a random subset or the easiest tasks? Could selection bias inflate the reported success rates?
What is the success rate of the pure retargeted policy without RL? This baseline would quantify the contribution of RL and the contact reward.

How are the keypoint-vertex contact pairs extracted in practice, and what fraction of frames yield no valid contact candidates due to noisy hand/object poses? How sensitive are results to the distance thresholds tau_j and the weighting factors lambda_c?
The imitation reward equation in Section 3.4 seems to use Delta_pos twice; should the second term be Delta_rot? Please clarify.
How are the wrist residual targets converted to joint angles via IK, and does the IK solver account for self-collision or arm posture beyond wrist position/orientation?
Does the pose-estimation comparison feed FoundationPose the same estimated depth (VGGT) or ground-truth depth? How are object masks provided to each baseline?
How does the policy performance degrade if ground-truth hand poses are used instead of HaMeR estimates, isolating the impact of hand pose noise?
Why is there no comparison with other RGB-video-based methods such as OKAMI or DexMV in the full pipeline evaluation?
Limitations: The framework is developed and evaluated only in simulation; no physical robot deployment is attempted, leaving a substantial sim-to-real gap.
The assumptions are restrictive: single human demonstrator, rigid tabletop objects, and stationary camera; deformable or articulated objects are not supported.
Target objects are manually identified in the first frame, which limits full automation and scalability to unconstrained videos.
Hand and object poses are estimated sequentially and independently, which can produce inconsistent contact priors and propagate errors.
The contact reward can converge to local optima, especially for concave or hollow geometries, as shown in the shoe-picking failure case.
The end-effector control parameterization ignores full arm posture, which is important for collision avoidance and coordinated multi-arm manipulation.
Success rates on real and synthetic videos remain low (27.4% and 39.0%), and the reference object trajectory itself is noisy, limiting real-world applicability.
The pipeline is modular and may accumulate errors from each stage (reconstruction, pose estimation, retargeting, RL), but per-stage error contributions are not quantified.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, though advancing video-to-robot skill transfer could have dual-use implications.

Hand and object poses are estimated sequentially and independently, which can produce inconsistent contact priors and propagate errors.
The contact reward can converge to local optima, especially for concave or hollow geometries, as shown in the shoe-picking failure case.
The end-effector control parameterization ignores full arm posture, which is important for collision avoidance and coordinated multi-arm manipulation.
Success rates on real and synthetic videos remain low (27.4% and 39.0%), and the reference object trajectory itself is noisy, limiting real-world applicability.
The pipeline is modular and may accumulate errors from each stage (reconstruction, pose estimation, retargeting, RL), but per-stage error contributions are not quantified.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, though advancing video-to-robot skill transfer could have dual-use implications.
